# Crumbline Standing Orders

## Executive Summary

Crumbline's wholesale bakery customers currently place repeat orders via WhatsApp, forcing owners to manually re-key every order — consuming most of Sunday evenings per owner (PM-reported; exact hours TBD to validate) — with 1 in 9 wholesale orders last quarter containing a quantity error. This PRD defines **Standing Orders**: a feature letting wholesale buyers configure and self-edit recurring orders within a bakery-set cut-off window, eliminating manual re-keying and targeting an error rate below 1 in 40. Beta launches with 7 bakeries ahead of the spring menu change in March 2027.

---

## Problem Statement

- Bakeries receive repeat wholesale orders (from cafes, delis) via WhatsApp and re-key them manually every week
- Re-keying consumes **most of Sunday evening** per owner (PM-reported; exact hours are unvalidated — see Next Steps)
- **1 in 9** wholesale orders last quarter contained a wrong quantity
- Buyers operate on a **9 pm–5 am** window — outside staffed bakery hours — with no self-service channel, forcing them onto the phone

**Root cause:** No structured channel exists for buyers to manage repeat orders, making the owner a manual data-entry bottleneck and a single point of failure for accuracy.

**Identified gap:** Total weekly wholesale order volume is unknown. This baseline is needed to size error counts and calculate error rate improvement in absolute terms. Recommend extracting from Crumbline's order logs before development kick-off.

---

## Target Users

### Persona 1 — Bakery Owner / Shift Lead
- Manages orders and production planning across 1–3 shops
- Spends most of Sunday evening re-entering orders already received via WhatsApp
- Primary device: shop tablet; needs offline capability in connectivity-limited production areas

### Persona 2 — Wholesale Buyer (Cafe / Deli Purchaser)
- Orders between **9 pm and 5 am** — outside bakery staffed hours
- Has no order confirmation or audit trail today; relies entirely on WhatsApp threads
- **Assumption to validate:** primarily mobile device; confirm in discovery

---

## Goals & Success Metrics

| Goal | Metric | Target |
|---|---|---|
| Reduce order errors | Wrong-quantity orders as share of all wholesale orders | < 1 in 40 (from 1 in 9) |
| Reduce owner re-keying effort | Weekly time on wholesale order entry | **Target:** ≥ 70% reduction vs. baseline (assumption — validate after time-diary study) |
| Buyer self-service | % of orders placed/edited without owner involvement | **Target:** ≥ 80% (assumption — validate) |
| Reduce phone contacts | Support contacts per order cycle | **Target:** < 0.05 per order (assumption — validate) |

---

## Detailed Requirements

### Functional Requirements

**Buyer-facing**
- **FR-01:** Buyer creates a standing order template from the bakery's product catalogue
- **FR-02:** Buyer edits quantities up to the bakery-set cut-off; blocked with a clear message after cut-off
- **FR-03:** Buyer receives in-app confirmation with a timestamp when an order locks
- **FR-04:** Buyer can skip a single week without deleting the standing order
- **FR-05:** Buyer views order history for the past **Assumption: 13 weeks** (validate preferred lookback with beta users)

**Owner-facing**
- **FR-06:** Owner sets a weekly cut-off day and time, globally or per buyer
- **FR-07:** Owner sees a consolidated order view per production day with quantities summed by product
- **FR-08:** Owner can manually override a locked order; all overrides logged with timestamp and actor
- **FR-09:** Owner receives a push + in-app alert when a standing order is edited within **Assumption: 2 hours** of cut-off
- **FR-10:** Owner marks products as unavailable for a specific week (required before spring menu change)
- **FR-11:** Unavailable products are shown to buyers as unavailable — not silently hidden — to prevent surprise gaps

### Non-Functional Requirements

- **NFR-01 (Offline):** Full read/write on the shop tablet; edits queue locally and sync on reconnect with no data loss
- **NFR-02 (Availability):** **Target:** 99.5% uptime during 9 pm–5 am buyer window (assumption — validate with engineering)
- **NFR-03 (Performance):** Order confirmation rendered in < 2 seconds on a 4G connection (assumption — validate)
- **NFR-04 (Data integrity):** Offline conflicts resolved last-write-wins + conflict flag for owner review; no silent discard
- **NFR-05 (Accessibility):** Buyer mobile UI meets WCAG 2.1 AA

---

## User Stories & Acceptance Criteria

**US-01 — Buyer edits a standing order**
> As a wholesale buyer, I want to adjust quantities before cut-off so my delivery matches this week's needs.
- **AC:** Before cut-off — save updates the order and shows a confirmation timestamp.
- **AC:** After cut-off — edit attempt shows a clear cut-off message; no changes are saved.

**US-02 — Owner views consolidated orders**
> As a bakery owner, I want all standing orders in one view after cut-off so I can plan production without re-keying.
- **AC:** Post-cut-off, all locked orders appear in a single list sortable by product, with per-product totals.

**US-03 — Offline order access**
> As a shift lead on the shop tablet, I want to access and confirm orders with no Wi-Fi so a network outage doesn't stop production.
- **AC:** With no connectivity, last-synced data is accessible; any edits queue for sync and are applied without data loss on reconnect.

**US-04 — Owner sets cut-off**
> As an owner, I want to set a weekly cut-off so buyers know the deadline.
- **AC:** Saving a cut-off time updates all linked buyers' views without requiring a support action.

---

## Scope

### In Scope
- Standing order create, edit, lock by cut-off
- Skip-week without deletion
- Owner consolidated order view + manual override with audit trail
- Product availability toggling
- Offline read/write on tablet with sync
- Beta with 7 bakeries before March 2027 spring menu change

### Out of Scope
- Invoicing, payment, delivery routing
- New buyer account creation (**Assumption:** buyers already have Crumbline accounts — validate)
- Multi-currency or tax calculation

---

## Technical Considerations

- **Offline-first:** Requires a local datastore (e.g., SQLite or IndexedDB) with a defined conflict-resolution strategy. **Gap:** Confirm whether Crumbline's existing API supports offline sync or requires a new layer — flag as engineering sprint 1 discovery item.
- **Cut-off enforcement:** Server-authoritative; client UI must reflect server time, not device clock, to prevent bypass.
- **Notification load:** Push infrastructure must handle concurrent buyer activity during the 9 pm–5 am window; test delivery latency before beta.
- **Tablet UX:** Large tap targets, high contrast — legible in a kitchen environment under low light.
- **Hard dependency:** FR-10/FR-11 (product unavailability) must be in beta before the spring menu change.

---

## Risks & Mitigations

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Offline sync conflicts corrupt orders | Medium | High | Server-authoritative cut-off; conflict flag + owner override (FR-08) |
| Buyers miss cut-off, blame bakery | High | Medium | In-app countdown; push reminder at Assumption: 1 hour prior |
| Beta bakeries have varied catalogue structures | Medium | Medium | Discovery workshop with all 7 bakeries in Week 1 |
| March deadline slips under heavy beta feedback | Medium | High | Feature freeze on standing-order core by end of January 2027; post-beta changes go to v1.1 |
| Low buyer adoption keeps owners on WhatsApp | Medium | High | Owners send a personal onboarding message to each buyer; track weekly adoption during beta |

---

## Timeline & Milestones

| Milestone | Target Date |
|---|---|
| Discovery complete (time-diary, buyer device audit, API sync gap) | 2026-11-28 |
| Engineering kick-off + schema design finalized | 2026-12-05 |
| Alpha: standing order create/edit + cut-off (online only) | 2027-01-09 |
| Offline sync layer complete | 2027-01-23 |
| Beta launch — 7 bakeries | 2027-02-06 |
| Beta feedback freeze (no new features) | 2027-02-27 |
| Spring-menu-change-ready release | 2027-03-14 |

**Note:** "March" is assumed to mean March 2027 based on today's date of 2026-11-04. Confirm with stakeholders.

---

## Next Steps

1. **Validate the error-rate baseline** — Pull last-quarter wholesale order logs from Crumbline to confirm the 1-in-9 figure and establish absolute order volume needed for target-setting.
2. **Run owner time-diary study** — 2-week diary with 3–5 bakery owners to quantify Sunday evening hours; use as the denominator for the 70% reduction target.
3. **Buyer device audit** — Survey buyers at all 7 beta bakeries to confirm mobile-first assumption and scope offline requirements accurately.
4. **Engineering API gap analysis** — Determine by 2026-11-28 whether offline sync extends the existing Crumbline API or requires a new layer; output a build-vs-extend decision.
5. **Beta bakery kick-off workshop** — 90-minute session with all 7 bakeries to align on catalogue structure, cut-off preferences, and beta success criteria before development starts.
6. **Confirm March year** — Align with stakeholders on whether "spring menu change in March" is March 2027 and lock the hard release date.

# Crumbline Q1 Retention

## Executive Summary

Crumbline enters the 6 January – 28 March quarter with 238 paying bakeries, $612K ARR, and a 94% net revenue retention rate — a meaningful gap from the 100%+ NRR that signals true expansion-led growth. The PM's own observation identifies the highest-leverage retention driver available: bakeries that set up wholesale ordering in their first month stay far longer. This OKR set targets three reinforcing bets — accelerating wholesale activation for new bakeries, recovering revenue from bakeries that have already churned to the free plan, and reframing "ship offline tablet mode" around the customer outcome it is meant to produce. Several KR targets below depend on baselines that have not yet been pulled (current wholesale activation rate, free-plan bakery count, connectivity ticket volume); those figures are explicitly labelled as targets or assumptions and **must be validated by 10 January** before commitments are finalised with the team.

---

## Cycle Details

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Start** | 6 January |
| **End** | 28 March |
| **Length** | 12 weeks |
| **Team** | 5 engineers, 1 designer, 2 customer success leads |
| **Hiring constraint** | No new hires until April |

---

## OKR Set

### Objective 1 — New bakeries achieve a wholesale ordering win in their first 30 days

*Turn the onboarding window into Crumbline's primary retention engine by making wholesale activation the default first success moment for every new bakery.*

- **KR 1.1** Raise the share of new bakeries that place their first wholesale order within 30 days of signup to **Target: 70%** by 28 March. *Assumption: current baseline is unknown — pull from product analytics before 10 January and revise the target accordingly.*
- **KR 1.2** Reduce the median days-to-first-wholesale-order for bakeries onboarded during the quarter to **Target: ≤ 14 days**. *Assumption: current median is unknown; baseline required.*
- **KR 1.3** Both customer success leads complete a structured wholesale-activation check-in with **100%** of new bakeries within their first 10 days of signup, for every cohort starting in January and February.
- **KR 1.4 (learning KR)** Measure and document a directional retention-rate difference between bakeries activated to wholesale in month one versus those who are not, using cohorts onboarded this quarter. *Purpose: validate the assumed causal link and anchor Q2 quantitative targets. Note: 12-week cohort sizes may be too small for statistical significance; treat this as a signal KR, not a proof.*

---

### Objective 2 — Recover revenue from bakeries that downgraded to the free plan

*Win back bakeries that already know Crumbline — the highest-probability re-conversion pool this quarter, requiring zero product discovery from the customer.*

- **KR 2.1** Reactivate **Target: 20 bakeries** from the free plan to any paid tier by 28 March. *Assumption: total count of bakeries currently on the free plan is unknown. If CS pulls the free-plan list and it contains fewer than ~40 bakeries, 20 may be sandbagged; revise upward or downward once the list is in hand.*
- **KR 2.2** Recover **Target: $51,420** in annualised recurring revenue from win-back conversions by 28 March. *This is an estimate computed as 20 bakeries (Target: KR 2.1) × $2,571 average ARR per bakery ($612K ÷ 238 paying bakeries). The result is an estimate, not a data-backed figure, because both inputs carry assumptions.*
- **KR 2.3** Achieve a **Target: 40%** positive-response rate on outbound win-back outreach sequences run by the two CS leads. *Assumption: no prior win-back campaign data exists; 40% is a target to validate, not a reference rate.*

---

### Objective 3 — Crumbline works reliably for bakeries regardless of internet connectivity

*Remove connectivity as a reason to avoid or abandon Crumbline — especially for bakeries running front-of-house tablets in environments with unreliable Wi-Fi.*

> **⚠ Output-to-outcome reframe:** The original goal "ship offline tablet mode" is an output (a feature delivered), not an outcome (a customer result). The objective above reframes it around bakery reliability. Shipping the feature becomes KR 3.1; adoption and reduced friction are KRs 3.2–3.3.

- **KR 3.1** Ship offline tablet mode to 100% of paying bakeries by **Target: 28 February** — four weeks before cycle end, preserving time within the quarter to observe adoption. *Assumption: engineering estimates this as achievable in the quarter; confirm with the engineering lead by 10 January. If the date slips to late March, KRs 3.2–3.3 become unscorable this cycle.*
- **KR 3.2** Achieve **Target: 30%** of tablet-active bakeries enabling offline mode within 21 days of release. *Assumption: count of tablet-active bakeries is unknown; retrieve from product analytics before locking this target.*
- **KR 3.3** Reduce support tickets tagged "connectivity" or "sync" by **Target: 50%** compared to the equivalent 12-week period preceding this cycle. *Assumption: current connectivity ticket volume is unknown; baseline before 10 January.*

---

## Expert Analysis & Gaps

### 🔴 Flags: sandbagging and measurability risks

- **Missing baselines are the single greatest risk this quarter.** KRs 1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 3.2, and 3.3 all require data that has not been pulled. Targets set without baselines are almost always sandbagged or unmeasurable. The team has until 10 January to close this gap before OKRs should be treated as committed.
- **KR 2.1 (20 bakeries) is explicitly a placeholder** and must be revisited once the free-plan cohort size is known.
- **KR 1.4 is a learning KR, not a committed KR.** Label it accordingly so it is not scored against the team as a miss.

### 🟡 Gaps the PM did not address

- **No NRR target stated for the quarter.** All three objectives drive retention, yet there is no stated goal for where NRR lands by 28 March. Without a guiding number, mid-cycle trade-off decisions lack a tiebreaker. Recommend adding an NRR guardrail at the company level (see below).
- **Team allocation is unresolved.** Offline tablet mode is the most engineering-intensive objective. If it absorbs three or more engineers, the in-product onboarding improvements needed to move KRs 1.1 and 1.2 will stall. Explicitly allocate engineers to objectives in week one.
- **CS leads face a split-focus problem.** Running simultaneous inbound activation check-ins (KR 1.3) and outbound win-back campaigns (KRs 2.3) with the same two people risks degrading both. A written workload split — including time allocation — should be agreed before 13 January.
- **No wholesale-flow friction audit planned.** Activation improvement cannot be achieved by CS effort alone if the wholesale setup UI is confusing. The designer's first assignment should be an audit of the wholesale ordering setup flow before any code is written.

---

## Alignment with Company-Level OKRs

The three Q1 objectives collectively target a single company-level outcome: **raise NRR above 94%**. Oakhollow Software should have an explicit company-level OKR such as:

> **Company Objective:** Make Crumbline indispensable to every independent bakery that uses it
> **Company KR:** Raise NRR from 94% to **Target: TBD** by [company fiscal year end — not provided by PM; treat as an assumption to confirm]

The Q1 OKRs nest as follows:

- **Obj 1 (activation)** → directly reduces early-cohort churn, the primary NRR drag at 94%
- **Obj 2 (win-back)** → recovers revenue from lapsed accounts, expanding the paying-bakery base from 238
- **Obj 3 (offline mode)** → removes a product gap that may be driving free-plan downgrades

If Oakhollow has existing company-level OKRs, map each KR to its parent before finalising. If not, propose the company-level NRR OKR this quarter.

---

## Next Steps

1. **By 10 January — Pull all baselines.** Wholesale activation rate, median time-to-first-order, free-plan bakery count, tablet-active bakery count, and connectivity ticket volume. No KR target is trustworthy without these numbers.
2. **By 10 January — Engineering feasibility confirmation on offline tablet mode.** Confirm the feature ships by 28 February. If not, revise KR 3.1 and accept that KRs 3.2–3.3 will not be scoreable this cycle.
3. **By 10 January — Designer wholesale flow audit starts.** Identify UI/UX friction in the wholesale setup path before any engineering work is scoped for Objective 1.
4. **By 13 January — Revise all placeholder targets.** Once baselines exist, revisit KRs 1.1, 1.2, 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 3.2, and 3.3 for sandbagging. Targets that cannot stretch should be explained, not quietly left soft.
5. **By 13 January — Written CS workload split.** Agree and document exactly how the two CS leads divide time between activation (KR 1.3) and win-back (KR 2.3), including hours or percentage allocation per week.
6. **By 13 January — Engineer-to-objective allocation.** Assign named engineers to Objectives 1 and 3 to surface contention early rather than at the mid-cycle review.
7. **Target: week 6 (~17 February) — Mid-cycle OKR score.** Assumption: a mid-cycle review is planned; confirm the date and format with the team. At this point, KR 3.1 (offline mode) should already be shipped or on track, and win-back response data (KR 2.3) will indicate whether the 20-bakery reactivation target is achievable.

# Why Care Homes Adopt Shiftnest

## Executive Summary

Based on 10 discovery calls with registered managers of small care homes (15–60 staff) conducted this year, three overlapping crises drive adoption of Shiftnest: unplanned out-of-hours staffing emergencies, unsustainable agency spend, and compliance vulnerability exposed during regulatory inspections. All three converge on a single root cause — rota data living in fragmented, uncontrolled spreadsheets. Seven of the 10 managers interviewed relied on emailed spreadsheets as their primary scheduling tool, creating multiple conflicting versions and no reliable audit trail. The functional job Shiftnest is hired to do is: *give me one authoritative rota I can act on and hand to an inspector at any moment.* The emotional job is to eliminate the late-night dread of unknown gaps. This analysis maps the full job landscape, defines hiring criteria, names the competing solutions being fired, and identifies the triggers that convert tolerance into purchase. It concludes with specific research gaps and prioritised next steps for Bramblegate's website rewrite and first-week setup checklist.

---

## Functional Jobs

### Primary Job

**When** an open shift appears at short notice — including late at night — **I want to** identify and confirm available cover without making a cascade of phone calls, **so I can** maintain safe staffing ratios and stop working from my kitchen table at midnight.

### Supporting Jobs

- **When** an inspector requests the current rota, **I want to** produce a single, timestamped, authoritative version immediately, **so I can** demonstrate compliance without searching email threads or reconciling conflicting copies.
- **When** deciding whether to call an agency or push a shift to an existing employee, **I want to** see the cost difference in real time, **so I can** make the cheapest safe decision quickly rather than defaulting to agency out of habit.
- **When** a staff member requests a shift swap, **I want to** approve or decline it in one step with the rota updating automatically, **so I can** stop manually editing and re-emailing a spreadsheet every time something changes.
- **When** planning the week ahead, **I want to** see which staff are approaching overtime or contracted-hours limits, **so I can** prevent compliance breaches before they occur.

---

## Emotional Jobs

- **When** I am running a home largely on my own, **I want to** feel genuinely in control of who is working each shift, **so I can** stop carrying a background anxiety about unknown gaps that surfaces every evening.
- **When** an inspection is announced — or arrives unannounced — **I want to** feel confident my records are clean and consistent, **so I can** face the inspector without fear that a rota discrepancy will call my competence into question.
- **When** a midnight staffing crisis forces me to my kitchen table, **I want to** resolve it in minutes, **so I can** feel like a manager rather than a 24/7 on-call dispatcher.

---

## Social Jobs

- **When** regulators review my records, **I want to** present a professionally managed, audit-ready staffing operation, **so I can** protect my registration and the home's reputation.
- **When** I report to the home owner or operator, **I want to** show concrete evidence that I am controlling agency spend, **so I can** demonstrate my value and justify any technology investment.
- **When** recruiting or retaining care staff, **I want to** offer a transparent, mobile-accessible scheduling experience, **so I can** reduce no-shows caused by shift confusion from outdated spreadsheets.

---

## Hiring Criteria

These are the criteria managers use — consciously or not — to decide whether Shiftnest earns the job:

| Criterion | Why it matters (from calls) |
|---|---|
| **Single source of truth** | "Three versions" of the rota was cited as a direct compliance risk |
| **Speed to fill a gap** | Midnight incidents set the bar: resolution must be faster than phoning a list of staff and an agency |
| **Mobile accessibility for staff** | Managers cannot fill gaps if staff cannot see or respond to open shifts from their phones |
| **Visible agency-vs-in-house cost** | Agency staff cost "more than the building"; managers need a reason to choose in-house first |
| **Audit trail and instant export** | Inspector-ready rota output is a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have |
| **Low setup friction** | Small care homes have no IT function; a setup process that runs beyond a week risks abandonment |

---

## Competing Solutions Being Fired

These are the tools and behaviours Shiftnest displaces at the moment of adoption:

- **Emailed spreadsheet rota** — used by 7 of 10 managers interviewed. Fired because it produces multiple versions, requires a manual re-send after every change, and leaves no audit trail.
- **WhatsApp group for last-minute changes** — common complement to the spreadsheet. Fired (or demoted) because messages get buried in chat history and shift confirmations are informal and unverifiable.
- **Phone calls to the agency** — the default gap-fill method at midnight. Fired for high cost and dependence on a human intermediary being available out of hours.
- **Paper rota on a noticeboard** — present in some homes as the "official" version even when a spreadsheet exists. Fired because it cannot be accessed remotely and drifts from the digital copy.
- **Generic scheduling tools not built for care** — fired because they lack care-specific compliance fields and do not account for contracted-hours rules relevant to the sector.

---

## Switching Triggers

Managers tolerate a painful status quo for a long time. These are the specific events that break that tolerance:

1. **A midnight gap-filling incident** — explicitly named in the calls. The moment a manager is at the kitchen table at midnight with no cover confirmed is the moment they begin searching for an alternative.
2. **An inspection that exposes rota inconsistencies** — being asked for the rota and producing three versions is a credibility and compliance crisis. For the managers who experienced this, it was a point of no return.
3. **An agency invoice that shocks** — when the monthly agency bill visibly exceeds a level the manager or owner can no longer rationalise, cost pain converts to action.
4. **A staff no-show caused by a scheduling error** — when someone fails to appear because they had the wrong shift from an outdated spreadsheet, the error becomes visible, attributable, and no longer deniable.

---

## Research Gaps & Recommendations

### Gaps Identified

- **Sample size**: 10 calls is a strong qualitative start but insufficient to weight which trigger is most common. No quantitative frequency data exists yet.
- **Frontline staff perspective is absent**: The mobile accessibility criterion and staff-side scheduling experience are inferred from manager comments — no calls with care workers were conducted.
- **Post-adoption outcomes are unknown**: There is no data on actual agency cost reduction, time saved per week, or compliance outcomes after adopting Shiftnest. These figures are essential for website copy.
- **Price sensitivity is uncharted**: Managers were previously paying effectively zero for a spreadsheet. Assumption to validate: switching cost perception may be the primary barrier for homes still evaluating.
- **Decision authority is unclear**: It is unknown whether registered managers purchase independently or need owner/operator sign-off, which directly affects both sales motion and website messaging.

### Recommendations for the Website Rewrite

## Executive Summary

Shiftnest's payroll export must go live on 1 April — a fixed, immovable deadline coinciding with the UK tax year start — serving 126 care homes across three payroll providers. The combination of one untestable provider integration, midnight-crossing shift logic diverging per provider, two engineers (one part-time), and no dedicated QA creates a high-probability scenario for pay errors at scale on day one. Because hours worked feed directly into staff pay, any export error translates immediately to underpayment or overpayment of care workers, with downstream exposure to regulatory inspection failures and potential data-protection breaches. Five risks score 50 or above on a severity × likelihood (S×L) matrix (scores are computed from the PM's inputs; see methodology below), warranting mitigation owners and hard deadlines before 1 April.

---

## Risk Scoring Methodology

**RPN = Severity (S) × Likelihood (L)**, each rated 1–10.
- **High:** RPN ≥ 50 — escalate immediately, assign owner
- **Medium:** RPN 25–49 — mitigate before launch
- **Low:** RPN < 25 — monitor

*Detection (D) dimension omitted to stay concise; treat all High items as having low detectability unless a testing gate is added.*

---

| ID | Risk | Failure Mode | Effect on Care Homes / Staff | S | L | RPN | Rating |
|----|------|-------------|------------------------------|---|---|-----|--------|
| R01 | Untested payroll provider integration | No test environment → format/logic errors undetected pre-launch | Pay file rejected or silently wrong; staff at affected homes underpaid | 9 | 8 | **72** | 🔴 HIGH |
| R02 | Midnight-shift hour-split divergence | Three providers split cross-midnight shifts differently; Shiftnest uses one rule | Night-shift hours miscounted; systematic over/underpayment | 9 | 8 | **72** | 🔴 HIGH |

| R05 | Regulatory non-compliance | Exported records differ from approved hours; regulator inspection fails | Enforcement action against care homes; Shiftnest contractual liability | 10 | 5 | **50** | 🔴 HIGH |
| R06 | Employee ID / field-mapping mismatch | Staff IDs or cost-centre codes differ between Shiftnest and provider schemas | Hours exported against wrong employee record | 9 | 5 | **45** | 🟡 MEDIUM |
| R07 | Payroll file format rejection | Schema version, delimiter, or encoding mismatch per provider | Payroll run delayed; staff paid late | 8 | 5 | **40** | 🟡 MEDIUM |

### R01 — Untested Provider Integration

- **Owner:** Lead engineer | **Deadline:** Target: 20 March

5. **Provider contract SLA for 1 April:** No mention of whether providers guarantee availability on the tax-year-start date, which is a peak processing day. Obtain written confirmation or a contingency window.

# Shiftnest North Star

## Executive Summary

Shiftnest's subscription revenue has a clear structural protector: care homes that fill ≥70% of their open shifts through the platform rarely cancel. Today's aggregate fill rate of 41% means most homes are well below that retention threshold, creating significant churn risk and capping growth. This document defines **Homes at 70%+ Fill Rate** as Shiftnest's single North Star Metric — a count that cannot be gamed by outlier homes masking a struggling long tail — and identifies four input metrics each team can own to close the 29-percentage-point gap. Three critical data gaps (home-level distribution, shift leakage source, and causality direction of the 70% threshold) must be resolved before any targets become hard commitments; all figures presented here are proposed targets or labeled assumptions, pending a home-level audit.

---

## North Star Metric

**Homes at 70%+ Fill Rate**

*Definition:* The number of active care homes in which ≥70% of their open shifts — across a rolling 28-day window — are filled by own staff through Shiftnest.

**Why this metric:**
- The 70% threshold is the PM-stated inflection point where homes rarely cancel — the strongest available signal of delivered value and of protected recurring revenue
- Counting homes (not averaging rates) prevents a handful of highly engaged homes from masking a long tail of at-risk subscribers
- It reflects a real care-delivery outcome — reduced agency dependency — giving it meaning beyond finance and making it defensible to customers
- Every team has a clear line of sight: the metric moves only when homes cross the threshold, so contribution is unambiguous

*Current baseline:* The aggregate fill rate is **41%** across all homes. **Assumption: home-level distribution is unknown until a baseline audit is run.** Some homes may already exceed 70%; most likely do not.

---

## Input Metrics

### 1. Shift Posting Completeness
**Owner:** Customer Success
**Definition:** % of each home's open shifts posted to Shiftnest *before* any other channel (agency call, group chat, phone) is used.
**Why it matters:** A shift never posted to Shiftnest cannot be filled through it. If managers default to phoning an agency first, the 41% fill rate is a structural ceiling regardless of product quality. This is the upstream constraint — and the most critical unknown.
**Current state:** Unknown. **This is the highest-priority data gap.**

### 2. Staff Readiness Rate
**Owner:** Onboarding / Product
**Definition:** % of rostered staff per home who are app-active (at least one login in the past 28 days) and have shift-swap notifications enabled.
**Why it matters:** Even with 100% of shifts posted, they can only be claimed if staff are reachable. Low readiness means posted shifts expire, managers lose trust, and they revert to phoning. This is the supply-side lever.
**Current state:** TBD — requires home-level instrumentation.

### 3. Posted Shift Claim Rate
**Owner:** Product
**Definition:** % of shifts posted to Shiftnest that are claimed by a staff member within an agreed time window. **Assumption: a meaningful window (e.g., 4 hours) must be validated with home managers — treat as a threshold to set, not a given.**
**Why it matters:** Claim speed is the trust signal that keeps managers on the platform. A slow or unclaimed shift triggers an agency call. This metric isolates whether platform mechanics — notifications, matching, UX — are working independently of posting and readiness.
**Current state:** TBD.

### 4. Homes Newly Crossing the 70% Threshold
**Owner:** Implementation / Customer Success
**Definition:** Count of homes that move from <70% to ≥70% fill rate in a given month for the first time.
**Why it matters:** The NSM stock only grows when homes cross the threshold. This flow metric holds CS accountable for active progression, not just churn prevention of homes already above 70%.
**Current state:** TBD pending baseline audit.

---

## Counter Metrics

| Counter Metric | Risk Being Guarded Against |
|---|---|
| **Agency spend per home (£/month)** | Fill rate rising but agency spend flat means homes are over-scheduling, not replacing agency |
| **Shift acceptance concentration** (% of shifts filled by the top 20% of staff per home) | Hitting 70% by burning out a small group of willing staff — unsustainable and a churn precursor |
| **Post-fill shift cancellation rate** | Staff claiming shifts and then cancelling inflates the fill rate without delivering real value |
| **Manager app session frequency** | If hitting 70% requires heavy manual admin, homes will abandon the platform; flag if sessions are rising without fill rate rising |

---

## Targets

| Metric | Current | Target | Timeframe |
|---|---|---|---|
| **NSM: Homes at ≥70% Fill Rate** | Unknown (Assumption: <20% of homes — validate in audit) | **Target: 50% of active homes** | **Target: 12 months from baseline audit date** |
| Shift Posting Completeness | Unknown | **Target: ≥85% per home** | **Target: 6 months** |
| Staff Readiness Rate | Unknown | **Target: ≥60% of rostered staff per home** | **Target: 6 months** |
| Posted Shift Claim Rate | Unknown | **Target: ≥75% within agreed claim window** | **Target: 9 months** |
| New Homes Crossing 70% | Unknown | **Target: set after audit establishes pipeline** | Rolling monthly |

*All targets are proposed and require validation against home-level data before they become commitments.*

---

## Initiatives Mapped to Input Metrics

### → Shift Posting Completeness
- **Platform-first SOP:** CS embeds Shiftnest as Step 1 in each home's shift-fill procedure with manager training. No home marked "fully onboarded" without documented SOP sign-off.
- **Agency bypass detection:** Instrument the platform to flag when a home has unfilled roster gaps but no corresponding Shiftnest post within an agreed lag window. CS receives an automated alert and follows up within 24 hours.

### → Staff Readiness Rate
- **Onboarding gates:** No home marked "live" until **Assumption: ≥50% of rostered staff** have completed first login and enabled notifications (threshold to validate with onboarding data).
- **Dormant staff re-engagement:** Automated push to staff with no login in 14 days, triggered at the moment their home manager posts the next shift.

### → Posted Shift Claim Rate
- **Preference-based notification routing:** Prioritize alerts to staff who have previously accepted similar shifts (same role, same day pattern) before broadcasting to all eligible staff.
- **Urgency cueing:** Surface time-remaining prominently in notifications for shifts within the agreed claim window of their start time, where agency escalation risk is highest.

### → Homes Newly Crossing 70%
- **70% Progress Dashboard:** Real-time per-home rolling 28-day fill rate with RAG status. CS reviews all amber homes (50–69%) weekly and executes a defined intervention playbook.
- **Milestone playbook:** CS defines scripted interventions at 30%, 50%, and 65% fill rate to move homes through the funnel systematically, not reactively.

---

## Identified Gaps

Three gaps require resolution before strategy execution:

1. **No home-level fill rate distribution.** The 41% figure is an aggregate. Without knowing the spread across homes, the NSM baseline is an assumption and targets will be guesses.
2. **Leakage source is uninstrumented.** Some shifts bypass Shiftnest entirely; others are posted but unclaimed. These are fundamentally different problems requiring different fixes. The aggregate rate cannot distinguish them.
3. **The 70% threshold causality is unconfirmed.** Homes above 70% rarely cancel — but whether Shiftnest use *causes* retention or whether more engaged homes both use the platform more *and* churn less affects where to invest. Five CS interviews on each side of the threshold would surface this quickly.

---

## Next Steps

1. **Run a home-level fill rate audit (Weeks 1–2):** Pull per-home shift data to establish the actual NSM baseline, distribution, and how many homes are already above 70%. No target is credible without this.
2. **Instrument shift origin tracking (Weeks 1–4):** Distinguish shifts posted to Shiftnest from shifts that bypass it. This separates the posting problem from the matching problem and prioritises the fix.
3. **Conduct 10 CS qualitative interviews (Weeks 2–4):** 5 homes above 70%, 5 below 50%. Validate the 70% causal mechanism and identify the top reasons managers bypass the platform.
4. **Assign metric owners and set baselines (Week 3):** Each team owner formally accepts their input metric, defines instrumentation needed, and proposes a baseline-adjusted target for leadership review.
5. **Ship the 70% Progress Dashboard for CS (Month 2):** The operational tool that makes the NSM visible in daily CS work and enables proactive intervention on amber homes before they churn.

## Executive Summary

Pallet Pilot is slotting software built for small third-party logistics (3PL) operators running a single site with 5,000–40,000 pallet spaces — a segment routinely underserved by enterprise slotting tools and left to manage slot decisions through spreadsheets, WMS rules, or a floor lead's memory. # Shelf-Label "Baked Today" Time Test

## Executive Summary

Crumbline will run a two-arm experiment across its 412 shops to test whether adding a "baked today" timestamp to shelf labels increases daily sell-through rate above the PM-provided baseline of 82%. Under the assumption that shop-level sell-through rate has a standard deviation of 0.08 (historical data not yet pulled), the 412 available shops yield an estimated minimum detectable effect of **~2.2 percentage points** at 80% power—or require ~224 shops to detect a targeted 3 pp lift. The recommended test window is 4 weeks (a target, not a data-derived figure), starting on a Monday. The single most critical structural risk is multi-shop bakeries being split across arms, which can contaminate results; bakery-level randomization is strongly recommended. All sample size figures in this document are estimates contingent on assumed inputs.

---

## Hypothesis

**If** we print a "baked today" timestamp alongside the price on shelf labels, **then** the daily sell-through rate (share of each day's bake sold by closing) will increase above the 82% baseline, **because** an explicit freshness signal reduces end-of-day purchase hesitation and increases perceived product quality.

---

## Primary Metric

**Daily sell-through rate per shop**: units sold ÷ units baked that day, averaged across all days in the test window per shop.

- **Baseline**: 82% (PM-provided)
- **Direction**: increase

---

## Guardrail Metrics

| Metric | Purpose | Alert Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| Average daily bake volume per shop | Catch bakeries gaming sell-through by baking less | >5% drop vs. pre-test — **Target threshold, assumption** |
| Label reprint rate | Flag operational friction from timestamp format | Any statistically significant increase |
| Shop-initiated support tickets | Detect printing or configuration errors at scale | >2× pre-test rate — **Target threshold, assumption** |

---

## Minimum Detectable Effect

**Target MDE: 3 percentage points** (82% → 85%). This is a **target set for planning purposes — not provided by the PM**. The PM must confirm whether a 3 pp lift is the minimum commercially meaningful improvement before the test launches.

---

## Sample Size Calculation

### Inputs

| Input | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline sell-through rate (p) | 82% | PM-provided |
| MDE (δ) | 3 pp | **Target — assumption to validate with PM** |
| Significance level (α) | 0.05, two-tailed | **Assumption** |
| Statistical power (1−β) | 80% | **Assumption** |
| SD of shop-level sell-through (σ) | 0.08 | **Assumption — must be pulled from historical shop logs** |
| Variance (σ²) | 0.0064 | Computed from assumed σ |
| Randomization unit | Shop | PM-provided |
| Available shops | 412 (~206 per arm) | PM-provided |
| ICC (day-to-day within shop) | 0.15 | **Assumption — measure from historical daily logs** |
| Average items/day per shop | Unknown | **Assumption needed; PM gave range 40–900 only** |
| Test duration | 28 days | **Target — assumption** |
| Design effect (shop-day analysis) | 1 + (28−1) × 0.15 ≈ **5.05** | Computed from assumed ICC and assumed duration |

### Formula and Result

Using a two-sample t-test at the shop level (each shop's mean sell-through rate as the observation unit):

**n per arm = 2σ²(z_α/2 + z_β)² / δ²**
= 2 × 0.0064 × (1.96 + 0.84)² / (0.03)²
= 2 × 0.0064 × 7.84 / 0.0009
≈ **112 shops per arm → 224 shops total**

**This is an estimate** because σ = 0.08 is an assumption. With all 412 shops (~206 per arm), the achievable MDE at 80% power is approximately **2.2 percentage points — also an estimate, contingent on assumed σ = 0.08**. If σ = 0.10, required n rises to ~174 per arm, still within 206 available.

> **Design-effect warning**: if the analysis uses shop-day observations rather than shop-level means, the assumed ICC of 0.15 over 28 days inflates variance by ~5×, dramatically reducing effective sample size. Pre-specify the analysis unit before launch and validate ICC from historical data.

---

## Test Duration

**Recommended: 28 days (4 complete Monday–Sunday cycles).** This is a **target duration assumption** — not derived from traffic data (not provided).

- Covers day-of-week variation in bake volume and foot traffic
- Run must start on a Monday and end on a Sunday
- **No early stopping**: commit to a fixed end date. Any interim peek must use a pre-registered alpha-spending function (e.g., O'Brien-Fleming) or Type I error is inflated

---

## Randomization Unit

**Nominally: shop** (PM-specified, because labels print per shop).

**Critical structural risk**: 238 bakeries operate 412 shops — roughly 1.7 shops per bakery on average. If a bakery's shops are split across arms, bakery staff may change their overall workflow upon seeing one label format, contaminating both arms.

**Strong recommendation**: Randomize at the **bakery level**, assigning all shops of a given bakery to the same arm. This reduces the randomization pool to 238 bakeries (~119 per arm). Under assumed σ = 0.08 and target δ = 3 pp, 112 per arm is sufficient — 119 per arm just clears this threshold. **This is an estimate**: if σ > 0.083, bakery-level randomization will be underpowered and the PM must either accept a larger MDE or find additional bakeries.

If shop-level randomization is retained despite this risk, use **block randomization within bakeries** and **cluster standard errors at the bakery level** in analysis.

**Stratification**: Within whichever unit is randomized, stratify by shop size (small / medium / large) to prevent imbalance from the wide 40–900 items/day range. Define size buckets from the actual distribution — **the specific thresholds are a target assumption**.

---

## Analysis Plan

1. **Pre-test baseline**: pull 4 weeks of pre-experiment sell-through data per shop for covariate adjustment
2. **Primary estimator**: two-sample Welch's t-test on shop-level mean sell-through rate; use ANCOVA with baseline sell-through as covariate to reduce residual variance and increase power
3. **Clustered standard errors**: if shop-level randomization is used, cluster SEs at the bakery level
4. **Intention-to-treat (ITT)**: all randomized shops included regardless of label compliance
5. **Sensitivity check**: per-protocol analysis excluding shops with verified non-compliance (< 90% of days with correct label format — **90% is a target threshold, assumption**)
6. **Heterogeneity analysis**: report treatment effect split by shop size bucket; large shops (high volume) may show different dynamics than small shops
7. **Significance**: p < 0.05, two-tailed; confidence interval reported alongside p-value

---

## Potential Pitfalls

### 🚨 Multi-Shop Bakery Contamination (Highest Risk)
Addressed above. Resolve the randomization unit before any other planning step.

### Novelty Effect
Treatment shops may see a spike in week 1 as customers notice the new label. **Mitigation**: compare week 1–2 vs. week 3–4 effect sizes separately. A decaying effect suggests novelty, not a durable intervention.

### Simpson's Paradox
If large shops (high bake volume) cluster in one arm, aggregate sell-through comparisons will be misleading. **Mitigation**: stratified randomization + size-stratified analysis as a mandatory robustness check given the 40–900 items/day range.

### Day-of-Week Confounding
Sell-through almost certainly varies across the week. Running exactly 4 complete Monday–Sunday cycles eliminates this confounder; partial weeks introduce it.

### Label Compliance Drift
If shops disable the timestamp (e.g., formatting issues), ITT dilutes the true effect. Track daily compliance and report it as a secondary process metric.

---

## Next Steps

1. **[Immediate — before any randomization]** Confirm bakery-level vs. shop-level randomization with the PM and engineering team; this is the single highest-risk design decision.
2. **[Within 1 week]** Pull 8+ weeks of historical daily sell-through data per shop to measure σ and ICC empirically and replace assumed values in the sample size calculation.
3. **[Within 1 week]** Validate the 3 pp MDE target with the PM and finance team to confirm commercial significance.
4. **[Within 2 weeks]** Define shop size strata thresholds from the actual items-per-day distribution and implement stratified randomization in the assignment tool.
5. **[Before launch]** Pre-register the analysis plan (hypothesis, primary metric, analysis method, stopping rule) in an internal experiment registry to prevent post-hoc changes.
6. **[At launch]** Instrument label compliance tracking so per-protocol sensitivity analysis is possible at close-out.

# Shiftnest Open-Shift Offers — User Stories

## Executive Summary

Shiftnest's current open-shift process requires managers to phone staff individually — a time-intensive method that leaves shifts unfilled and burdens care-home leadership. This document defines the product backlog to replace that workflow with an in-app open-shift offer system: eligible workers see available shifts, the first to claim wins the shift, and a registered manager approves within **2 hours** (from PM input) or the system automatically re-offers. Stories are grouped into four epics covering Discovery, Claiming & Eligibility, Manager Approval, and Notifications. Five material gaps have been identified and require PM decisions before sprint planning begins.

---

## Epic 1: Open Shift Discovery

### Story 1.1 — Care Worker Views Available Open Shifts

**As a** care worker, **I want** to see all open shifts I am eligible for in the app, **so that** I can decide whether to claim one without waiting for a phone call.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
```gherkin
Given I am logged in as a care worker
  And at least one open shift exists for my site
When I navigate to the Open Shifts screen
Then I see each shift's date, start time, end time, ward/unit, and required role
  And I only see shifts for which I meet the training requirements
  And I only see shifts that would not breach my maximum weekly hours limit [TBD — see Gap 1]
```

---

### Story 1.2 — Shift Lead Views Open Shifts for Their Unit

**As a** shift lead, **I want** to see open shifts on my unit, **so that** I can monitor coverage gaps alongside the app doing the outreach.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
```gherkin
Given I am logged in as a shift lead
When I open the Open Shifts screen
Then I see all open shifts for units I am assigned to
  And each shift displays its current status: "Open", "Pending Approval", or "Filled"
```

---

## Epic 2: Shift Claiming & Eligibility Enforcement

### Story 2.1 — Eligible Worker Claims an Open Shift

**As a** care worker, **I want** to claim an open shift with a single tap, **so that** I can secure additional hours quickly before another colleague does.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
```gherkin
Given I am viewing an open shift I am eligible for
  And the shift status is "Open"
When I tap "Claim Shift" and confirm
Then my claim is recorded with a timestamp
  And the shift status changes to "Pending Approval"
  And the shift is no longer claimable by other workers
  And I see a confirmation message: "Claim submitted — awaiting manager approval"
```

---

### Story 2.2 — System Blocks Claim That Would Breach Maximum Weekly Hours

**As a** care worker, **I want** the app to prevent me from claiming shifts that would exceed my contracted maximum weekly hours, **so that** I stay compliant and avoid a manual rejection.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
```gherkin
Given my scheduled hours for the current week plus the open shift duration
  would exceed my maximum weekly hours [value TBD — see Gap 1]
When I tap "Claim Shift"
Then the claim is rejected immediately
  And I see a message: "This shift would exceed your weekly hours limit — claim not submitted"
  And no claim record is created
```

---

### Story 2.3 — System Blocks Claim Due to Missing Training

**As a** care worker, **I want** the app to prevent me from claiming a shift that requires a training certificate I do not hold, **so that** I am never placed in a role I am not qualified for.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
```gherkin
Given a shift requires one or more specific training certificates [list TBD — see Gap 2]
  And my profile is missing at least one of those certificates
When I attempt to claim the shift
Then the claim is blocked
  And I see which training requirement(s) I am missing
  And the shift remains "Open" for other workers
```

---

## Epic 3: Manager Approval Workflow

### Story 3.1 — Registered Manager Approves or Rejects a Claimed Shift

**As a** registered manager, **I want** to approve or reject a pending shift claim from within the app, **so that** I maintain oversight of staffing without managing phone calls.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
```gherkin
Given a care worker has claimed an open shift
  And the claim is in "Pending Approval" status
When I open the claim in the Manager dashboard
Then I see the worker's name, role, relevant training, and scheduled weekly hours
When I tap "Approve"
Then the shift status changes to "Filled" and the worker is confirmed
When I tap "Reject" and provide a reason
Then the shift returns to "Open" and is offered to other eligible workers
  And the worker is notified of the rejection with the reason given
```

---

### Story 3.2 — System Re-Offers Shift After 2-Hour Approval Window Expires

**As a** care worker, **I want** unclaimed approval decisions to time out automatically, **so that** an open shift is never stuck in limbo because a manager did not respond.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
```gherkin
Given a shift claim is in "Pending Approval" status
When exactly 2 hours pass without manager action
Then the claim is cancelled
  And the shift status returns to "Open"
  And the original claimant is notified: "Your claim expired — the shift is now available to others"
  And the manager receives a notification: "A pending claim expired on [shift date/time]"
```

---

## Epic 4: Notifications & Escalation

### Story 4.1 — Workers Receive Push Notification for New Open Shift

**As a** care worker, **I want** an instant push notification when a shift I am eligible for becomes available, **so that** I can claim it before colleagues who check the app less frequently.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
```gherkin
Given a registered manager publishes an open shift
When the shift is saved with status "Open"
Then all eligible workers receive a push notification within [Target: 30 seconds — assumption to validate]
  And the notification shows the shift date, time, and unit
  And tapping the notification opens the shift detail screen directly
```

---

### Story 4.2 — Manager Is Notified When a Shift Is Claimed

**As a** registered manager, **I want** an immediate in-app and push notification when a worker claims an open shift, **so that** I can review and approve within the 2-hour window.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
```gherkin
Given a care worker successfully claims an open shift
When the claim is submitted
Then the responsible registered manager receives a push notification within [Target: 30 seconds — assumption to validate]
  And the notification states the worker's name and shift details
  And the notification includes a deep link to the approval screen
```

---

## Gap Analysis & Expert Recommendations

| # | Gap | Impact | Recommended Action |
|---|-----|--------|--------------------|
| **1** | **Maximum weekly hours value not defined.** The PM confirms the rule exists but provides no figure. | Eligibility checks cannot be built. | PM to confirm the contractual or regulatory hour cap per worker type (e.g., full-time vs. part-time) before Sprint 1. |
| **2** | **Training certificate taxonomy undefined.** No list of which certificates map to which shift types. | Story 2.3 is unestimable without this. | PM to supply the training matrix or confirm it will be imported from an existing HR system. |
| **3** | **Offer ordering / fairness rules absent.** "First eligible person" favours workers who check the app most. No priority weighting (e.g., part-time hours first, then bank staff, then agency) is defined. | Risk of unfair distribution and worker complaints. | Decide whether a simple first-come-first-served model is acceptable or whether a queue/priority rule is needed. |
| **4** | **Escalation path if no one claims.** What happens after the shift expires unclaimed (once, twice, N times)? | Shift could go unfilled silently. | Define a maximum re-offer count and a fallback action (e.g., alert manager to call agency after Assumption: 3 failed cycles). |
| **5** | **Manager approval authority scope.** Can shift leads approve, or only registered managers? | Story 3.1 may need two variants. | PM to confirm approval rights per role before the epic is estimated. |

---

## Next Steps

1. **Resolve Gap 1 & 2 (this week):** PM to supply maximum weekly hours values and the training–shift-type matrix — both are sprint-blocking.
2. **Define offer fairness policy (this week):** Decide first-come-first-served vs. priority queue; document the decision as a business rule so Story 2.1 can be estimated.
3. **Confirm manager approval scope (before Sprint 1 planning):** Clarify whether shift leads hold approval authority; add a story variant if needed.
4. **Design the escalation path (before Sprint 2):** Agree the maximum re-offer count and fallback action for persistently unclaimed shifts.
5. **Validate notification latency target (Sprint 1 kickoff):** Confirm whether the **30-second** push notification target (assumption) is achievable with the chosen notification provider, and lock it into the DoD.

# Shiftnest Market Size

## Executive Summary

Based solely on figures provided by the PM, Shiftnest operates in a national market of **9,400 care homes** (15–60 staff), generating a Total Addressable Market (TAM) of **$35.0M ARR** at the stated $310/month price. The Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM) narrows to **$21.0M ARR** by focusing on the 60% of homes the PM identified as still running rotas on spreadsheets — the clearest near-term conversion target. The Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM) depends on sales capacity data not yet provided; using a **target** capture rate of 5% of SAM in Year 1 (an explicit assumption to be replaced with pipeline data), SOM reaches approximately **$1.05M ARR**, scaling to a **target** of **$2.52M ARR** (12% of SAM) by Year 3. The 60% spreadsheet figure signals an early-stage digitisation market — a large opportunity, but one whose pace of conversion carries timing risk investors will probe.

---

## TAM — Total Addressable Market

**Definition:** Revenue if every qualifying home on the national register subscribed to Shiftnest.

### Top-Down Calculation

| Input | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Homes on national register (15–60 staff) | 9,400 | PM (care regulator's public register) |
| Monthly price per home | $310 | PM |
| Months per year | 12 | — |
| **TAM (ARR)** | **$34,968,000 ≈ $35.0M** | Calculated |

### Bottom-Up Calculation

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Annual contract value (ACV) per home | $310 × 12 = **$3,720** |
| Total addressable homes | 9,400 |
| **TAM (ARR)** | **$34,968,000 ≈ $35.0M** |

Both approaches converge at **$35.0M ARR**, confirming internal consistency. The register count of 9,400 is the single most load-bearing input — any change in eligibility criteria or regulatory re-classification would directly shift TAM.

---

## SAM — Serviceable Addressable Market

**Definition:** Homes Shiftnest can realistically target near-term — specifically those still on spreadsheets, who face no incumbent vendor switching cost.

### Top-Down Calculation

| Input | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Spreadsheet-rota rate | 60% (3 in 5) | PM (sales call observation) |
| Spreadsheet-using homes | 9,400 × 60% = **5,640** | Calculated |
| Monthly price | $310 | PM |
| **SAM (ARR)** | 5,640 × $310 × 12 = **$20,980,800 ≈ $21.0M** | Calculated |

### Bottom-Up Calculation

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| ACV per home | $3,720 |
| Spreadsheet-using homes | 5,640 |
| **SAM (ARR)** | **$20,980,800 ≈ $21.0M** |

**Sensitivity check:** The 60% figure comes from Shiftnest's own sales calls, which may skew toward spreadsheet users (self-selection). If the true register-wide rate is 50%, SAM falls to **$17.5M**; if 70%, SAM rises to **$24.5M**. Validate before the investor meeting.

---

## SOM — Serviceable Obtainable Market

**Definition:** Revenue Shiftnest can capture within a defined period given real constraints: sales capacity, conversion rates, and competitive friction.

### Assumptions (All Require PM Validation)

- **Assumption A:** Sales capacity, demo-to-close conversion rate, and average sales cycle length — not provided; **TBD**
- **Assumption B:** Target capture rates — **5% of SAM in Year 1**, **9% in Year 2**, **12% in Year 3** — these are targets introduced for modelling; replace with a capacity-driven bottoms-up once pipeline data is available
- **Assumption C:** No customer churn modelled — churn rate is **TBD**
- **Assumption D:** Price held constant at $310/month throughout

### SOM Projections (Target Scenario)

| Year | Target % of SAM | Homes | ARR |
|---|---|---|---|
| Year 1 | 5% *(target)* | 282 | **$1,049,040 ≈ $1.05M** |
| Year 2 | 9% *(target)* | 508 | **$1,889,760 ≈ $1.89M** |
| Year 3 | 12% *(target)* | 677 | **$2,518,440 ≈ $2.52M** |

*All SOM figures are estimates derived from the assumed target capture rates above. They are not forecasts.*

---

## Growth Drivers

- **Large greenfield, zero incumbent displacement:** 5,640 spreadsheet-using homes require no paid-tool switching — the sale is productivity vs. inertia, which shortens the objection cycle.
- **Regulatory compliance pressure:** The national care regulator maintains a public register, signalling that homes operate under documentation obligations. Any tightening of rota or staffing standards would accelerate adoption. **Gap:** PM has not specified pending regulatory changes — surface this for investors.
- **Chain/group ownership multiplier:** If homes share group operators, one decision-maker could unlock multiple sites. **Gap:** PM has not stated whether any of the 9,400 are chain-owned — this could increase deal size and reduce cost of acquisition per home.
- **Price accessibility:** At $310/month ($3,720 ACV), the product likely falls below most formal procurement thresholds, enabling manager-led adoption without a lengthy approvals process. **Assumption:** Decision-maker authority threshold — **TBD**.

---

## Market Timing

- A **60% spreadsheet rate** signals an early digitisation phase, not a late-majority displacement cycle. This is the right time to establish switching costs (data history, trained staff workflows) before the market matures.
- **Upside:** Category leadership is still available; homes that adopt Shiftnest now are unlikely to re-evaluate for several years.
- **Risk:** If homes delay digitisation — due to budget cycles, management turnover, or low regulatory urgency — conversion timelines extend and capital efficiency worsens.
- **Gap:** The PM has not disclosed Shiftnest's current customer count or tenure. Without a traction baseline, investors cannot assess whether the 60% conversion story is confirmed by real pipeline velocity or still theoretical.

---

## Key Gaps & Risks

| Gap | Impact | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Current customer count unknown | Cannot demonstrate penetration traction | Add to investor deck immediately |
| Sales cycle length not stated | SOM timing is unanchored | Measure first-demo-to-contract across closed deals |
| Churn rate absent | Multi-year SOM may be overstated | Pull retention data from existing cohort |
| 40% of homes not on spreadsheets | Unknown — paid incumbent or other? | Segment; if on paid tools, switching cost is higher and SAM narrows |
| Chain/group ownership | 9,400 may overstate decision-maker count | Overlay ownership data on the register |
| Geographic expansion | One-country TAM ceiling of $35.0M | Define entry criteria for a second country |
| Pricing sensitivity | $310 is stated, not tested | Run price sensitivity with 10 active prospects |

---

## Next Steps

1. **Confirm current customer count** and compute implied penetration of the 9,400-home register — the most important data point before the investor meeting; it anchors all SOM claims in real traction.
2. **Replace assumed SOM capture rates** with a sales-capacity bottoms-up: active reps × closed deals per rep per month × $3,720 ACV — this removes the need to defend an assumed percentage.
3. **Validate the 60% spreadsheet figure** against a random sample of the register (not just sales-call contacts) to eliminate self-selection bias before citing it as market evidence.
4. **Identify chain/group-owned homes** in the register; if multi-site deals are viable, restate SAM by decision-maker unit rather than individual home.
5. **Measure and disclose sales cycle length and demo-to-close rate** — both are essential for investors to assess capital efficiency and forecast SOM timing.
6. **Pull churn data** from the existing cohort to stress-test multi-year ARR projections and present net revenue retention alongside gross ARR growth.
